analysis.one_liner: Doubles the child tax credit, makes it fully refundable for all families, and pays for it by raising the corporate tax rate.
analysis.headline: The bill died in the House Ways and Means Committee without a vote or hearing, four months before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would double the child tax credit to $2,000 per child, remove income limits on the credit, and make it fully refundable — meaning families with little or no income tax bill would get the full amount in cash. Today, low-income families get a reduced credit or nothing because of earnings rules. To pay for it, the bill raises the corporate income tax rate from 21% to 28%. It was referred to the Ways and Means Committee and died there without a hearing, markup, or vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Single-parent and low-income families gain the most. Because the bill repeals the earnings requirements and income limits and makes the credit fully refundable, parents who earn little or owe no income tax would receive the full $2,000 per child — the group the current rules shortchange. Families with children at nearly every income level below the top would see their credit increase [S2][S3].

how_it_helps.text: Doubles the per-child credit from $1,000 to $2,000.
Repeals the income limits and earnings-based phase-downs, so the credit phases out only for the highest incomes.

Makes the credit fully refundable, meaning families with little or no federal income tax liability — the lowest earners — receive the full amount, the change most associated with cutting child poverty.

analysis.who_pays: Corporations bear the direct cost: the bill raises the corporate income tax rate from 21% to 28% to fund the expanded credit [S2][S3]. To the extent corporate taxes are passed through to shareholders or workers, the burden falls partly on investors and employees.

drawbacks.text: The bill is paid for by raising the corporate income tax rate from 21% to 28%, a cost that some economists argue is passed on partly to workers through lower wages and to consumers through prices.
Doubling the base credit to $2,000 and making it fully refundable is expensive; the corporate rate increase alone may not fully offset the cost, and the bill does not name other revenue sources.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is large and targeted: fully refundable CTC payments sharply reduce child poverty, especially for single-parent families with little or no tax liability [S2][S3]. The cost is a higher corporate tax rate, which corporations may partly pass through to workers and consumers over time; honest supporters acknowledge some of the $1,000-credit increase's cost is offset by shifting that burden. On balance the design directs new revenue to families raising children rather than leaving the 2017 corporate rate cuts untouched.

outcome.mechanism: The House referred the bill to the Ways and Means Committee on the day it was introduced, and the committee never acted on it before the 118th Congress ended, so it expired without a vote.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on August 13, 2024, with three cosponsors, and referred to the House Ways and Means Committee.
The action history shows no further steps: no hearings, no markup, no floor vote; the bill died in committee when the Congress ended.
The bill would have made the $2,000 child tax credit fully refundable and repealed income limits, paid for by a corporate rate increase from 21% to 28%.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Corporations keep the 21% tax rate; low-income families do not get the expanded credit.

for.name: Rep. Katie Porter
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to double the child tax credit, make it fully refundable, and pay for it with a corporate rate increase.

for.name: Reps. Ayanna Pressley and Delia Ramirez

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.role: Committee of jurisdiction for tax bills
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and took no action — no hearing, no markup, no vote — before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: All three supporters were Democrats; the bill had no Republican cosponsors, and the Ways and Means Committee, where it died, never acted on it.

industries.note: The federal corporate rate would rise from 21% to 28% to pay for the expanded child credit [S2][S3]. Corporations and their shareholders bear the direct cost; the rate increase applies to taxable years after 2024 [S3].
